title: Minimize before you send
summary: Redact direct identifiers, review a retention design, and keep prompts and responses inside a defined boundary.

scenario.briefing: The health-center assistant sends a student's name, email, phone, and card number to a model vendor so it can draft an appointment reminder. Prompts are kept for two years and shared with a analytics tool. Redact the record before the request and decide what the system may retain.

objectives.description: Redact direct identifiers without losing the fields the task needs.
Identify retention and sharing problems in the design.
Explain minimization, purpose, retention, and vendor boundaries.

hints: Name the fields the task actually needs before redacting.
Replace direct identifiers with a fixed marker.
Do not mutate the caller's record.
Keep a purpose, a retention period, and a deletion path for anything stored.

misconceptions.description: Removing the name but leaving email, phone, and card data.
misconceptions.feedback: Email, phone, and card numbers identify a person too. Redact all direct identifiers the task does not need.

misconceptions.description: Retaining prompts indefinitely because storage is cheap.
misconceptions.feedback: Retention needs a purpose and a limit. Keep only what supports the task or a legal obligation, then delete it.

misconceptions.description: Treating redaction as a guarantee of anonymity.
misconceptions.feedback: Combined fields can re-identify a person even after direct identifiers are removed. Minimize the record and assess re-identification risk.

sections.title: Purpose decides the fields
sections.body: Start with the task: drafting an appointment reminder needs a time, a clinic, and perhaps a first name. It does not need a card number or a home address. Collect and send only what the purpose requires.

sections.title: Redaction is not deletion
sections.body: Replacing an email with a marker removes the direct identifier from the prompt but does not remove the original record. The source system still needs access control, and redaction rules must cover every direct identifier.

sections.title: Retention and vendors are part of the design
sections.body: Prompts and responses can contain personal data. Define why they are stored, how long, who can read them, and when they are deleted. A vendor is another boundary with its own retention and access.

steps.title: Redact the appointment record
steps.prompt: Edit privacy.js. redactPii(record) returns a new record with email, phone, and card replaced by "[redacted]". Keep every other field unchanged and do not mutate the input.
hints: Copy the record instead of editing it in place.
Replace only the three direct identifiers.
Leave missing fields missing rather than inventing values.
Return null for a null record and keep unrelated fields intact.

tests.description: Returns null for a null record.
tests.name: redactPii

steps.title: Review the retention design
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Ask why each stored field exists.
Look at the retention period and deletion path.
Check who else receives the prompts.
Reject the design: no purpose, long retention, vendor sharing, and no deletion.

artifact.title: Assistant data plan
artifact.caption: The retention section of the launch review.
artifact.content:
Storage: every prompt and response is kept for 730 days.
Purpose: "analytics and future product ideas".
Access: all staff can query the prompt table.
Vendor: prompts are forwarded to an analytics tool with an unlimited retention setting.
Deletion: no deletion path is implemented; rows are never removed.

findings.label: Prompts and responses are kept for two years without a task-based limit.
The stated purpose is broad and does not justify storing health-related text.
Prompts are forwarded to a vendor with unlimited retention.
There is no deletion path for stored prompts.
Cheap storage makes indefinite retention acceptable.

verdicts.label: Reject until purpose, access, retention, and deletion are defined

steps.explanation: Encryption does not justify keeping health data forever or sharing it without a purpose. Purpose, access, retention, and deletion all need limits.

steps.title: Keep the data boundary honest
hints: Start from the purpose, then list the fields.
A vendor is another processor with its own retention.
Redaction reduces but does not guarantee anonymity.
Select minimization, purpose, retention, access, and vendor controls; reject redaction as anonymity.

statements.label: The task purpose determines which fields may be sent.
Stored prompts need a retention period and a deletion path.
Only staff who need the data for the stated purpose should be able to read it.
A model or analytics vendor is another boundary with its own access and retention terms.
Redacting direct identifiers guarantees the remaining record is anonymous.

steps.explanation: Privacy depends on purpose, minimization, access, retention, deletion, and vendor terms. Redaction is one control, not a guarantee.

accessibility.summary: Every control is reachable by keyboard, and the checks report text results rather than color alone.
accessibility.keyboardNotes: Use Tab to move between controls. Space selects a choice, and Ctrl+Enter runs or submits the active check.
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: Each option, finding, and test announces its label, state, and whether the check passed.
